title: The strange thing about Balaam was never that he could not hear God.
paragraphs: The strange thing about Balaam was never that he could not hear God.
It was that he could.
That is what makes his story terrifying.

Not because he was spiritually deaf…
but because he was spiritually gifted while secretly in love with corruption.
There are people who think the greatest danger to the Church is atheism, witchcraft, or persecution.
Scripture reveals something even more dangerous:

a man who can speak prophetic words…
while his heart quietly bows to greed.
Balaam was not an ignorant pagan stumbling in darkness.
He heard the voice of the living God.
He received revelation.
He spoke accurate prophecy.
He even declared some of the most breathtaking messianic words in the Old Testament.

And yet…
the New Testament remembers him as a warning.
Not a hero.
Not a prophet of righteousness.
A warning.
That should shake every believer reading this.

Because Balaam proves a person can have spiritual experiences…
and still love sin more than truth.

And if that doesn’t humble us…
we have not understood his story yet.

In Numbers 22, Balak king of Moab becomes terrified because Israel is advancing through the wilderness after victories over enemy nations. Instead of repentance, Balak seeks spiritual manipulation. He sends for Balaam, a famous diviner from Pethor.
The Hebrew calls Balaam a qōsēm (קֹסֵם) — a diviner or occult practitioner.
Not a covenant prophet like Moses.
Not a priest of Yahweh.
A pagan spiritual specialist who somehow still had genuine encounters with the true God.
That alone should stop shallow theology in its tracks.
Because God is sovereign enough to speak even through compromised vessels.
Balak offers Balaam payment to curse Israel.
And immediately the rot inside Balaam begins to reveal itself.
Numbers 22:7 says:
“The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand.”
The Hebrew phrase is:

וּקְסָמִים בְּיָדָם
(u-qesamim b’yadam)

Literally:
“divination payments in their hands.”
Money was already attached to the assignment before Balaam ever prayed.
And that matters.
Because corruption often enters long before the compromise becomes visible.
Balaam asks God if he should go.
God says no.
Simple.
Clear.
Direct.
But Balaam’s heart had already leaned toward the reward.
This is where many believers misunderstand sin.
Sin rarely begins with rebellion.
It begins with desire.
A desire we refuse to crucify.
A craving we keep revisiting in prayer hoping God will eventually bless what He already condemned.
That is Balaam.
He keeps returning to the possibility because greed has already infected his spirit.
The Apostle Peter later exposes Balaam’s heart plainly:

“He loved the wages of unrighteousness.”
— 2 Peter 2:15
The Greek is devastating.

ἀγαπήσας μισθὸν ἀδικίας
(agapēsas misthon adikias)

Literally:
“having loved the payment of injustice.”
Not stumbled into it.
Not accidentally drifted.
Loved it.
That word agapaō (ἀγαπάω) is a strong word for love, attachment, affection.
Balaam’s issue was not confusion.
It was affection.
He loved what was corrupt.
And this is where the story stops feeling ancient and starts feeling terrifyingly modern.

Because there are people today who still know how to pray…
still know how to quote Scripture…
still know how to preach…
still know how to worship publicly…
yet privately love what God hates.
Some love money more than holiness.
Some love attention more than truth.
Some love lust more than purity.
Some love influence more than obedience.
And like Balaam, they keep standing near God’s voice while refusing to surrender their appetite.
Be honest.
That hits differently when you stop reading Balaam as “the villain” and realize Scripture preserved his story because human hearts still behave exactly like his.
Then comes one of the most haunting moments in the Bible.
God permits Balaam to go.
And people often misunderstand this passage.
Numbers 22:20 says:
“If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them…”
Yet only a few verses later God’s anger burns against Balaam for going.
Why?
Because divine permission is not always divine approval.
Sometimes God lets a person walk into the thing they insisted on pursuing.

Not because He endorses it…
but because stubborn hearts often learn only through exposure.

Romans 1 echoes this terrifying judgment:
“God gave them over…”
There comes a point where relentless compromise stops fighting conviction and starts silencing it.
Balaam had already chosen internally before he ever saddled the donkey.
And then comes the scene almost everyone remembers:
the talking donkey.
But most people miss the deeper horror.
The donkey sees the angel before Balaam does.
Think about that.

The spiritually celebrated man is blind…
while the animal sees clearly.
Numbers 22:31 says:
“Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam…”
The Hebrew:

וַיְגַל יְהוָה אֶת־עֵינֵי בִלְעָם
(vay’gal YHWH et-einei Bil‘am)
“YHWH uncovered Balaam’s eyes.”
Uncovered.
Meaning the problem was never God’s absence.
It was Balaam’s blindness.
Corruption blinds.
Greed blinds.
Hidden sin blinds.
You can become so consumed with what you want that you stop recognizing the sword directly in front of you.
And some people reading this are exhausted because deep down you know God has been trying to stop you for a long time.
Not to ruin you.
To save you.
But every warning feels inconvenient when desire is driving the heart.
The donkey crushes Balaam’s foot against a wall three times.
Three collisions.
Three mercies.
Three interruptions.
And still Balaam is angry.
That is another terrifying symptom of spiritual corruption:
resenting the very thing God used to protect you.
Some people are angry about closed doors that literally saved their lives.
Angry about relationships God blocked.
Angry about opportunities God destroyed.
Angry about delays that were actually mercy wearing painful clothing.
Then Balaam finally arrives before Balak.
And something astonishing happens.

Every time Balaam tries to curse Israel…
God forces blessing out of his mouth instead.
Why?
Because no corruption in man can overturn covenant promises from God.
And this is where the beauty of the Gospel starts breaking through the darkness of Balaam’s story.
Israel was flawed.
Messy.
Rebellious.
Imperfect.
Yet protected by covenant grace.
Balaam could not destroy what God had chosen.

Child of God…
that matters more than you know.
Because hell has spoken curses over your life too.
Shame cursed you.
Addiction cursed you.
People cursed you.
Your past cursed you.
Your failures cursed you.
But when Jesus Christ covers someone by grace, the enemy cannot reverse what God has redeemed.
That is why Balaam’s prophecies become unexpectedly messianic.
In Numbers 24:17 Balaam declares:

“I see him, but not now…
a star shall come out of Jacob,
and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.”
The Hebrew says:

דָּרַךְ כּוֹכָב מִיַּעֲקֹב
(darakh kokhav mi-Ya‘aqov)
“A star shall march forth from Jacob.”
Early Jewish interpreters and later Christians both saw messianic significance here.
Even Balaam — compromised, greedy Balaam — became an unwilling witness pointing toward the coming King.
Jesus Christ.
Because God’s sovereignty is so overwhelming that even corrupted mouths can still end up announcing His glory.
But Balaam’s story does not end in redemption.
That is the tragedy.

Many people know the donkey story…
but forget the ending.
Unable to curse Israel directly, Balaam eventually teaches Moab how to destroy Israel spiritually.
Revelation 2:14 exposes it clearly:
“He taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel.”
The Greek phrase:

βαλεῖν σκάνδαλον
(balein skandalon)
“To throw a trap.”

Balaam realized if Israel could not be cursed externally…
they could still be corrupted internally.
So he weaponized seduction.
Idolatry.
Compromise.
Sexual immorality.
And thousands died.
This is why Balaam becomes one of Scripture’s most sobering symbols.
Not because he lacked spiritual exposure.
But because he refused full surrender.
There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who know Christian language but still secretly negotiate with sin.
Still bargaining.
Still delaying repentance.
Still protecting hidden compromise.
Still loving what destroys them.
And eventually hidden corruption always demands a price.
Jude 1:11 warns about:
“the error of Balaam.”
Not atheism.
Not ignorance.
Error.
Spiritual distortion fueled by selfish desire.
This is why the fear of the Lord matters.
Because gifts cannot replace holiness.
Revelation cannot replace obedience.
Charisma cannot replace repentance.
Knowledge cannot replace surrender.
You can impress crowds and still grieve God.
You can sound anointed and still be spiritually dying.
You can hear God’s voice and still refuse His authority.
Balaam’s life screams a warning across generations:
Do not confuse spiritual exposure with spiritual transformation.

One of the most heartbreaking realities in human existence is that a person can stand near holy things…
without ever becoming holy themselves.
Judas walked with Jesus and still betrayed Him.
The Pharisees memorized Scripture and still crucified Messiah.
Balaam heard God and still loved corruption.
And maybe the reason this article feels uncomfortable is because the Holy Spirit is exposing something deeper than information.
Maybe this is about us.
About the hidden compromise nobody sees.
About the appetite we keep excusing.
About the sin we keep spiritualizing.
About the private corruption hiding beneath public Christianity.
The beautiful thing about Jesus Christ is this:
He does not merely expose corruption.
He offers deliverance from it.
The Gospel is not behavior management.
It is heart transformation.
Ezekiel 36:26 says God gives a new heart.
Not improved corruption.
A new heart.
That means nobody reading this is beyond redemption.
Not the addicted.
Not the hypocrite.
Not the secret sinner.
Not the compromised believer.
Not the exhausted churchgoer pretending everything is fine.
Jesus still heals what surrender places in His hands.
But Balaam’s story warns us that partial surrender is still rebellion.
Delayed repentance is still danger.
And hidden compromise eventually becomes open destruction.

So tonight…
ask yourself honestly:
What do I secretly love more than obedience to God?
Because that was Balaam’s real downfall.
Not lack of revelation.
Misplaced love.
And if this exposed something hidden inside you, don’t run from conviction.
Run toward Christ.
Some people are not destroyed because they never heard God…
They are destroyed because they kept hearing Him while loving something else more.
